e-12525.knowledge_point: Calculating the Work Done by a Force
e-12525.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $3\,\rm{kg}$ moves along the $x$-axis with an acceleration of magnitude $(1 + 2x^2)\,\rm{m/s}^2$ acting in the direction $OP.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=0$ to $x=2.$
e-12525.worked_solution:
The work done by a force $F=F(x)$ in moving a particle from $x=x_1$ to $x=x_2$ is given by

$$
W = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} F(x) \,\textrm{d}x.
$$

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($\rm{J}$).

Using Newton's second law of motion, the force required to accelerate a particle of mass $3\,\rm{kg}$ at a rate of $(1 + 2x^2)\,\rm{m/s}^2$ is

$$
F = ma = 3 \cdot (1 + 2x^2) = (3 + 6x^2) \,\rm{N}.
$$

Now, substituting the known values into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(3+6{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[3x+2{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =3(2)+2({2}^{3})-(3(0)+2({0}^{3})) \\  & =6+16-0 \\  & =22\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

e-12526.knowledge_point: Calculating the Kinetic Energy of a Particle
e-12526.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $2\,\rm{kg}$ moves along the $x$-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude $(4t+1)\,\rm{m/s}^2,$ where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing $x,$ and $t \geq 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the change in kinetic energy of the particle between the times $t = 1\,\rm{s}$ and $t = 2\,\rm{s}.$
e-12526.worked_solution:
The change in kinetic energy of a particle with mass $m,$ initial velocity $v_0,$ and final velocity $v_1$ is given by

$$
\Delta \, \text{KE} = \dfrac{1}{2}mv_{1}^{2} - \dfrac{1}{2}mv_{0}^{2}.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($\rm{J}$).

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int (4t+1)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =2{t}^{2}+t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0) = 0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0 = 2(0^2) + 0 + C
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
C = 0.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t) = 2t^2 + t.$ In particular, its inital velocity at time $t = 1\,\rm{s}$ and final velocity at time $t = 2\,\rm{s}$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{0} & =v(1)=2({1}^{2})+1=3\,m/s, \\ {v}_{1} & =v(2)=2({2}^{2})+2=10\,m/s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change in kinetic energy of the particle between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ\,\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot {10}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot {3}^{2} \\  & =100-9 \\  & =91\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

e-12527.knowledge_point: Applying the Work-Energy Principle To Find the Work Done by a Force
e-12527.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $1\,\rm{kg}$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a resultant force. The displacement of the particle is given by $(t^2-2t+3)\,\rm{m},$ where $t \geq 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the work done by the force between the times $t=1\,\rm{s}$ and $t=3\,\rm{s}.$
e-12527.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W
= 
\Delta\, \text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
\Delta\, \text{KE} = \dfrac12 m v_1^2 - \dfrac12 m v_0^2
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, $v_0$ is its initial velocity, and $v_1$ is its final velocity.

The displacement of the particle is given by $x(t)=t^2-2t+3,$ where $t$ is time in seconds.
We find the velocity $v(t)$ of the particle by differentiating the displacement with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-2t+3) \\  & =2t-2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the particle's initial velocity, at $t=1$, is

$$
v_0 = v(1) =  2(1) -2 = 0\,\rm{m/s},
$$

and its final velocity, at $t=3$, is

$$
v_1 = v(3) = 2(3) -2= 4\,\rm{m/s}.
$$

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =Δ\,\text{KE} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot (4)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot {0}^{2} \\  & =8-0 \\  & =8\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

e-12528.knowledge_point: Applying the Work-Energy Principle to Find a Particle's Velocity
e-12528.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $2\,\rm{kg}$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a force of magnitude $(x+3)\,\rm{N}$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, and the particle has velocity $v=2\,\rm{m/s}$ at $x=2,$ calculate the velocity of the particle at $x=4.$
e-12528.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W
= 
\Delta\, \text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
\Delta\, \text{KE} = \dfrac12 m v_1^2 - \dfrac12 m v_0^2
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, $v_0$ is its initial velocity, and $v_1$ is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=2$ to $x=4{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{4}(x+3)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+3x]}_{2}^{4} \\  & =(8+12)-(2+6) \\  & =12\,J\end{aligned}
$$

The particle has velocity $v=2\,\rm{m/s}$ at $x=2.$ So, we can find the velocity $v_1$ at $x=4$ using the work-energy principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\ 12 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot {v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot {2}^{2} \\ 12 & ={v}_{1}^{2}-4 \\ {v}_{1}^{2} & =16 \\ {v}_{1} & =\pm 4.\end{aligned}
$$

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration. 

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at $x=4$ is $4\,\rm{m/s}.$

before.html:
Question 2
?

A particle P moves along the x-axis under the action of a force of magnitude 2x2N acting in the direction of increasing x. Given that x is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from x=0 to x=1.

a
1J
b
32J
c
2J
d
3J
e
23J
Submit

decision.explanation: Work is the integral of force over displacement: W=∫₀¹2x² dx=[2x³/3]₀¹=2/3 J.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a force of magnitude $2{x}^{2}\,\text{N}$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=0$ to $x=1.$
after.worked_solution:
The work done by a force $F=F(x)$ in moving a particle from $x={x}_{1}$ to $x={x}_{2}$ is given by

$$
W={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($J$).

Substituting the given values into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}(1-0) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

A particle P of mass 2.5kg moves along the x-axis with an acceleration of magnitude (4−x2)m/s2 acting in the direction OP. Given that x is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from x=0 to x=1.

a
172J
b
556J
c
8J
d
9J
e
212J
Submit

decision.explanation: The force is F(x)=ma=2.5(4-x²). Therefore W=∫₀¹2.5(4-x²) dx=2.5[4x-x³/3]₀¹=2.5(4-1/3)=55/6 J.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $2.5\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis with an acceleration of magnitude $(4-{x}^{2})\,{m/s}^{2}$ acting in the direction $OP.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=0$ to $x=1.$
after.worked_solution:
The work done by a force $F=F(x)$ in moving a particle from $x={x}_{1}$ to $x={x}_{2}$ is given by

$$
W={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($J$).

Using Newton's second law of motion, the force required to accelerate a particle of mass $2.5\,kg$ at a rate of $(4-{x}^{2})\,{m/s}^{2}$ is

$$
F=ma=2.5\cdot (4-{x}^{2})=(10-2.5{x}^{2})\,N.
$$

Now, substituting the known values into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(10-2.5{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[10x-\frac{5}{6}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(10(1)-\frac{5}{6}({1}^{3}))-(10(0)-\frac{5}{6}({0}^{3})) \\  & =10-\frac{5}{6} \\  & =\frac{55}{6}\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

A particle P of mass 2.5kg moves along the x-axis with an acceleration of magnitude (4−x2)m/s2 acting in the direction OP. Given that x is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from x=0 to x=1.

a

b
556J
c
8J
d
9J
e
212J
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The work done by a force F=F(x) in moving a particle from x=x1 to x=x2 is given by W=∫x1x2F(x)dx.

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules (J).

Using Newton's second law of motion, the force required to accelerate a particle of mass 2.5kg at a rate of (4−x2)m/s2 is F=ma=2.5⋅(4−x2)=(10−2.5x2)N.

Now, substituting the known values into our integral, we obtain W=∫01(10−2.5x2)dx=[10x−56x3]01=(10(1)−56(13))−(10(0)−56(03))=10−56=556J.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Work Done by a Force
content.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $2.5\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis with an acceleration of magnitude $(4-{x}^{2})\,{m/s}^{2}$ acting in the direction $OP.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=0$ to $x=1.$
content.worked_solution:
The work done by a force $F=F(x)$ in moving a particle from $x={x}_{1}$ to $x={x}_{2}$ is given by

$$
W={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($J$).

Using Newton's second law of motion, the force required to accelerate a particle of mass $2.5\,kg$ at a rate of $(4-{x}^{2})\,{m/s}^{2}$ is

$$
F=ma=2.5\cdot (4-{x}^{2})=(10-2.5{x}^{2})\,N.
$$

Now, substituting the known values into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(10-2.5{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[10x-\frac{5}{6}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(10(1)-\frac{5}{6}({1}^{3}))-(10(0)-\frac{5}{6}({0}^{3})) \\  & =10-\frac{5}{6} \\  & =\frac{55}{6}\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a force of magnitude $\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{N}$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=4.$
after.worked_solution:
The work done by a force $F=F(x)$ in moving a particle from $x={x}_{1}$ to $x={x}_{2}$ is given by

$$
W={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($J$).

Substituting the given values into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{x}\,{|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =-(\frac{1}{4}-1) \\  & =-(-\frac{3}{4}) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

A particle P moves along the x-axis under the action of a force of magnitude 1x2N acting in the direction of increasing x. Given that x is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from x=1 to x=4.

a
2J
b
12J
c
14J
d
34J
e
3J
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The work done by a force F=F(x) in moving a particle from x=x1 to x=x2 is given by W=∫x1x2F(x)dx.

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules (J).

Substituting the given values into our integral, we obtain W=∫141x2dx=−1x|14=−(14−1)=−(−34)=34J.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms W=∫₁⁴x⁻² dx=[-1/x]₁⁴=1-1/4=3/4 J, which is option d.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Work Done by a Force
content.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a force of magnitude $\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{N}$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=4.$
content.worked_solution:
The work done by a force $F=F(x)$ in moving a particle from $x={x}_{1}$ to $x={x}_{2}$ is given by

$$
W={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($J$).

Substituting the given values into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{x}\,{|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =-(\frac{1}{4}-1) \\  & =-(-\frac{3}{4}) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

A particle P of mass 4kg moves along the x-axis with an acceleration of magnitude (1x+x3)m/s2 acting in the direction OP. Given that x is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from x=1 to x=e.

a
(e4+3)J
b
4(e4+1)J
c
(e4+1)J
d
(2e4+3)J
e
4e4J
Submit

decision.explanation: F(x)=ma=4/x+4x³. Hence W=∫₁ᵉ(4/x+4x³) dx=[4 ln(x)+x⁴]₁ᵉ=4+e⁴-1=e⁴+3 J.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $4\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis with an acceleration of magnitude $(\frac{1}{x}+{x}^{3})\,{m/s}^{2}$ acting in the direction $OP.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=e.$
after.worked_solution:
The work done by a force $F=F(x)$ in moving a particle from $x={x}_{1}$ to $x={x}_{2}$ is given by

$$
W={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($J$).

Using Newton's second law of motion, the force required to accelerate a particle of mass $4\,kg$ at a rate of $(\frac{1}{x}+{x}^{3})\,{m/s}^{2}$ is

$$
F=ma=4(\frac{1}{x}+{x}^{3})=(\frac{4}{x}+4{x}^{3})\,N.
$$

Now, substituting the known values into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{1}^{e}(\frac{4}{x}+4{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[4\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+{x}^{4}]}_{1}^{e} \\  & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡e+{e}^{4}-(4\operatorname{ln}⁡1+{1}^{4}) \\  & =4+{e}^{4}-0-1 \\  & =({e}^{4}+3)\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

A particle P of mass 4kg moves along the x-axis with an acceleration of magnitude (1x+x3)m/s2 acting in the direction OP. Given that x is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from x=1 to x=e.

a
(e4+3)J
b
4(e4+1)J
c
(e4+1)J
d
(2e4+3)J
e
4e4J
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The work done by a force F=F(x) in moving a particle from x=x1 to x=x2 is given by W=∫x1x2F(x)dx.

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules (J).

Using Newton's second law of motion, the force required to accelerate a particle of mass 4kg at a rate of (1x+x3)m/s2 is F=ma=4(1x+x3)=(4x+4x3)N.

Now, substituting the known values into our integral, we obtain W=∫1e(4x+4x3)dx=[4ln⁡|x|+x4]1e=4ln⁡e+e4−(4ln⁡1+14)=4+e4−0−1=(e4+3)J.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Work Done by a Force
content.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $4\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis with an acceleration of magnitude $(\frac{1}{x}+{x}^{3})\,{m/s}^{2}$ acting in the direction $OP.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=e.$
content.worked_solution:
The work done by a force $F=F(x)$ in moving a particle from $x={x}_{1}$ to $x={x}_{2}$ is given by

$$
W={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($J$).

Using Newton's second law of motion, the force required to accelerate a particle of mass $4\,kg$ at a rate of $(\frac{1}{x}+{x}^{3})\,{m/s}^{2}$ is

$$
F=ma=4(\frac{1}{x}+{x}^{3})=(\frac{4}{x}+4{x}^{3})\,N.
$$

Now, substituting the known values into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{1}^{e}(\frac{4}{x}+4{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[4\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+{x}^{4}]}_{1}^{e} \\  & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡e+{e}^{4}-(4\operatorname{ln}⁡1+{1}^{4}) \\  & =4+{e}^{4}-0-1 \\  & =({e}^{4}+3)\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

A particle P of mass 85kg moves along the x-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude 3tm/s2, where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing x, and t≥0 is the time in seconds. Calculate the change in kinetic energy of the particle between the times t=1s and t=2s.

a
12J
b
36J
c
24J
d
27J
e
16J
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating a(t)=3t with v(0)=0 gives v(t)=3t²/2. Thus v(1)=3/2 and v(2)=6 m/s. The kinetic energy change is (1/2)(8/5)(6²-(3/2)²)=27 J.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $\frac{8}{5}\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude $3t\,{m/s}^{2},$ where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing $x,$ and $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the change in kinetic energy of the particle between the times $t=1\,s$ and $t=2\,s.$
after.worked_solution:
The change in kinetic energy of a particle with mass $m,$ initial velocity ${v}_{0},$ and final velocity ${v}_{1}$ is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($J$).

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int 3t\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0=\frac{3}{2}({0}^{2})+C\,⟹\,C=0.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}.$ In particular, its inital velocity at time $t=1\,s$ and final velocity at time $t=2\,s$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{0} & =v(1)=\frac{3}{2}({1}^{2})=\frac{3}{2}\,m/s, \\ {v}_{1} & =v(2)=\frac{3}{2}({2}^{2})=6\,m/s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change in kinetic energy of the particle between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ\,\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{8}{5}\cdot {6}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{8}{5}\cdot {(\frac{3}{2})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{144}{5}-\frac{9}{5} \\  & =27\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

The change in kinetic energy of a particle with mass m, initial velocity v0, and final velocity v1 is given by ΔKE=12mv12−12mv02.

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules (J).

First, we find v(t) by integrating the acceleration with respect to time: v(t)=∫a(t)dtv(t)=∫3tdtv(t)=32t2+C

Therefore, the change in kinetic energy of the particle between these times is ΔKE=12mv12−12mv02=12⋅85⋅62−12⋅85⋅(32)2=1445−95=27J.

Question 8
?

A particle P of mass 3kg moves along the x-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude 12t2m/s2, where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing x, and t≥0 is the time in seconds. Calculate the change in kinetic energy of the particle between the times t=1s and t=2s.

a
116J
b
218J
c
4J
d
154J
e
3J
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating a(t)=t²/2 with v(0)=0 gives v(t)=t³/6. Thus v(1)=1/6 and v(2)=4/3 m/s. The kinetic energy change is (3/2)((4/3)²-(1/6)²)=21/8 J.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $3\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude $\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}\,{m/s}^{2},$ where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing $x,$ and $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the change in kinetic energy of the particle between the times $t=1\,s$ and $t=2\,s.$
after.worked_solution:
The change in kinetic energy of a particle with mass $m,$ initial velocity ${v}_{0},$ and final velocity ${v}_{1}$ is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($J$).

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int \frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\frac{1}{6}{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0=\frac{1}{6}({0}^{3})+C\,⟹\,C=0.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{1}{6}{t}^{3}.$ In particular, its inital velocity at time $t=1\,s$ and final velocity at time $t=2\,s$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{0} & =v(1)=\frac{1}{6}({1}^{3})=\frac{1}{6}\,m/s, \\ {v}_{1} & =v(2)=\frac{1}{6}({2}^{3})=\frac{4}{3}\,m/s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change in kinetic energy of the particle between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ\,\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot {(\frac{4}{3})}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot {(\frac{1}{6})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}-\frac{1}{24} \\  & =\frac{21}{8}\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

A particle P of mass 3kg moves along the x-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude 12t2m/s2, where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing x, and t≥0 is the time in seconds. Calculate the change in kinetic energy of the particle between the times t=1s and t=2s.

a
116J
b
218J
c
4J
d
154J
e
3J
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The change in kinetic energy of a particle with mass m, initial velocity v0, and final velocity v1 is given by ΔKE=12mv12−12mv02.

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules (J).

First, we find v(t) by integrating the acceleration with respect to time: v(t)=∫a(t)dtv(t)=∫12t2dtv(t)=16t3+C

To determine C, we use the fact that v(0)=0. Substituting this into the above gives 0=16(03)+C⟹C=0.

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time t is v(t)=16t3. In particular, its inital velocity at time t=1s and final velocity at time t=2s are v0=v(1)=16(13)=16m/s,v1=v(2)=16(23)=43m/s.

Therefore, the change in kinetic energy of the particle between these times is ΔKE=12mv12−12mv02=12⋅3⋅(43)2−12⋅3⋅(16)2=83−124=218J.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms v(t)=t³/6. Hence ΔKE=(1/2)(3)((4/3)²-(1/6)²)=8/3-1/24=21/8 J, matching option b.

content.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $3\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude $\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}\,{m/s}^{2},$ where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing $x,$ and $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the change in kinetic energy of the particle between the times $t=1\,s$ and $t=2\,s.$
content.worked_solution:
The change in kinetic energy of a particle with mass $m,$ initial velocity ${v}_{0},$ and final velocity ${v}_{1}$ is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($J$).

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int \frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\frac{1}{6}{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0=\frac{1}{6}({0}^{3})+C\,⟹\,C=0.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{1}{6}{t}^{3}.$ In particular, its inital velocity at time $t=1\,s$ and final velocity at time $t=2\,s$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{0} & =v(1)=\frac{1}{6}({1}^{3})=\frac{1}{6}\,m/s, \\ {v}_{1} & =v(2)=\frac{1}{6}({2}^{3})=\frac{4}{3}\,m/s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change in kinetic energy of the particle between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ\,\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot {(\frac{4}{3})}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot {(\frac{1}{6})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}-\frac{1}{24} \\  & =\frac{21}{8}\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Integrating a(t)=1+t² with v(0)=0 gives v(t)=t+t³/3. Thus v(1)=4/3 m/s, and KE=(1/2)(6)(4/3)²=16/3 J.

after.name: Question 9
after.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $6\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude $(1+{t}^{2})\,{m/s}^{2},$ where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing $x,$ and $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the particle's kinetic energy at time $t=1\,s.$
after.worked_solution:
The kinetic energy of a particle with mass $m$ and velocity $v$ is given by

$$
\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2}.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($J$).

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int (1+{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =t+\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0=0+\frac{1}{3}({0}^{3})+C\,⟹\,C=0.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=t+\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}.$ In particular, its velocity at time $t=1\,s$ is

$$
v=v(1)=1+\frac{1}{3}({1}^{3})=\frac{4}{3}\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, the kinetic energy of the particle at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 6\cdot {(\frac{4}{3})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 6\cdot \frac{16}{9} \\  & =\frac{16}{3}\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

Correct

The kinetic energy of a particle with mass m and velocity v is given by KE=12mv2.

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules (J).

First, we find v(t) by integrating the acceleration with respect to time: v(t)=∫a(t)dtv(t)=∫(1+t2)dtv(t)=t+13t3+C

To determine C, we use the fact that v(0)=0. Substituting this into the above gives 0=0+13(03)+C⟹C=0.

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time t is v(t)=t+13t3. In particular, its velocity at time t=1s is v=v(1)=1+13(13)=43m/s.

before.html:
Question 10
?

A particle P of mass 4kg moves along the x-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude t3m/s2, where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing x, and t≥0 is the time in seconds. Calculate the particle's kinetic energy at time t=2s.

a
18J
b
32J
c
24J
d
12J
e
36J
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating a(t)=t³ with v(0)=0 gives v(t)=t⁴/4. Thus v(2)=4 m/s, and KE=(1/2)(4)(4²)=32 J.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $4\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude ${t}^{3}\,{m/s}^{2},$ where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing $x,$ and $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the particle's kinetic energy at time $t=2\,s.$
after.worked_solution:
The kinetic energy of a particle with mass $m$ and velocity $v$ is given by

$$
\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2}.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($J$).

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int {t}^{3}\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\frac{1}{4}{t}^{4}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0=\frac{1}{4}(0)^{4}+C\,⟹\,C=0.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{1}{4}{t}^{4}.$ In particular, its velocity at time $t=2\,s$ is

$$
v=v(2)=\frac{1}{4}({2}^{4})=4\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, the kinetic energy of the particle at $t=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {4}^{2} \\  & =32\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

A particle P of mass 4kg moves along the x-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude t3m/s2, where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing x, and t≥0 is the time in seconds. Calculate the particle's kinetic energy at time t=2s.

a
18J
b
32J
c
24J
d
12J
e
36J
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The kinetic energy of a particle with mass m and velocity v is given by KE=12mv2.

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules (J).

First, we find v(t) by integrating the acceleration with respect to time: v(t)=∫a(t)dtv(t)=∫t3dtv(t)=14t4+C

To determine C, we use the fact that v(0)=0. Substituting this into the above gives 0=14(0)4+C⟹C=0.

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time t is v(t)=14t4. In particular, its velocity at time t=2s is v=v(2)=14(24)=4m/s.

Therefore, the kinetic energy of the particle at t=2 is KE=12mv2=12⋅4⋅42=32J.

before.html:
Question 11
?

A particle P of mass 2kg moves along the x-axis under the action of a resultant force. The particle's velocity is 2tm/s, where t≥0 is the time in seconds. Calculate the work done by the force between the times t=1s and t=2s.

a
12J
b
4J
c
10J
d
16J
e
8J
Submit

decision.explanation: By the work-energy principle, W=(1/2)m(v(2)²-v(1)²). Since v(t)=2t, the velocities are 4 and 2 m/s, so W=(1/2)(2)(16-4)=12 J.

after.name: Question 11
after.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $2\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a resultant force. The particle's velocity is $2t\,m/s,$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the work done by the force between the times $t=1\,s$ and $t=2\,s.$
after.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

The particle's velocity is given by $v(t)=2t,$ where $t$ is time in seconds. So, the particle's initial velocity, at $t=1$, is

$$
{v}_{0}=v(1)=2(1)=2\,m/s,
$$

and final velocity, at $t=2$, is

$$
{v}_{1}=v(2)=2(2)=4\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =Δ\,\text{KE} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot (4)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot (2)^{2} \\  & =16-4 \\  & =12\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 11
?

A particle P of mass 2kg moves along the x-axis under the action of a resultant force. The particle's velocity is 2tm/s, where t≥0 is the time in seconds. Calculate the work done by the force between the times t=1s and t=2s.

a
12J
b
4J
c
10J
d
16J
e
8J
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

W=ΔKE

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

ΔKE=12mv12−12mv02

and m is the particle's mass, v0 is its initial velocity, and v1 is its final velocity.

The particle's velocity is given by v(t)=2t, where t is time in seconds. So, the particle's initial velocity, at t=1, is v0=v(1)=2(1)=2m/s, and final velocity, at t=2, is v1=v(2)=2(2)=4m/s.

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

W=ΔKE=12⋅2⋅(4)2−12⋅2⋅(2)2=16−4=12J.

content.knowledge_point: Applying the Work-Energy Principle To Find the Work Done by a Force
content.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $2\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a resultant force. The particle's velocity is $2t\,m/s,$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the work done by the force between the times $t=1\,s$ and $t=2\,s.$
content.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

The particle's velocity is given by $v(t)=2t,$ where $t$ is time in seconds. So, the particle's initial velocity, at $t=1$, is

$$
{v}_{0}=v(1)=2(1)=2\,m/s,
$$

and final velocity, at $t=2$, is

$$
{v}_{1}=v(2)=2(2)=4\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =Δ\,\text{KE} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot (4)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot (2)^{2} \\  & =16-4 \\  & =12\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

b
280J
c
242J

decision.explanation: Integrating acceleration and using v(0)=1 gives v(t)=t³+4t+1. Thus v(1)=6 and v(2)=17 m/s. By the work-energy principle, W=(1/2)(2)(17²-6²)=253 J.

after.name: Question 12
after.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $2\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a resultant force. The particle's acceleration is $(3{t}^{2}+4)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=1\,m/s$ when $t=0\,s,$ calculate the work done by the force between the times $t=1\,s$ and $t=2\,s.$
after.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

The acceleration of the particle is given by $a(t)=3{t}^{2}+4,$ where $t$ is time in seconds.
We find the velocity $v(t)$ of the particle by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (3{t}^{2}+4)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{3}+4t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
1=(0)^{3}+4(0)+C\,⟹\,C=1.
$$

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)={t}^{3}+4t+1.$
In particular, the particle's initial velocity, at $t=1,$ is

$$
{v}_{0}=v(1)=(1)^{3}+4(1)+1=6\,m/s,
$$

and final velocity, at $t=2,$ is

$$
{v}_{1}=v(2)=(2)^{3}+4(2)+1=17\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =Δ\,\text{KE} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot {17}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot {6}^{2} \\  & =289-36 \\  & =253\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

A particle P of mass 6kg moves along the x-axis under the action of a resultant force. The particle's acceleration is (12t+1)m/s2, where t≥0 is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity v=2m/s when t=0s, calculate the work done by the force between the times t=1s and t=4s.

a
160J
b
81J
c
144J
d
125J
e
96J
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

W=ΔKE

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

ΔKE=12mv12−12mv02

and m is the particle's mass, v0 is its initial velocity, and v1 is its final velocity.

The acceleration of the particle is given by a(t)=12t+1, where t is time in seconds. We find the velocity v(t) of the particle by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫(12t+1)dt=t+t+C

To determine C, we use the fact that v(0)=2. Substituting this into the above gives

2=0+0+C⟹C=2.

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at time t is v(t)=t+t+2. In particular, the particle's initial velocity, at t=1, is v0=v(1)=1+1+2=4m/s, and final velocity, at t=4, is v1=v(4)=4+4+2=8m/s.

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

W=ΔKE=12⋅6⋅82−12⋅6⋅42=192−48=144J.

Question 14

A particle P of mass 1kg moves along the x-axis under the action of a resultant force. The particle's velocity is (t+1)m/s, where t≥0 is the time in seconds. Calculate the work done by the force between the times t=2s and t=4s.

a
9J
b
8J
c
16J
d
17J
e
25J
Submit

decision.explanation: The velocities are v(2)=3 and v(4)=5 m/s. By the work-energy principle, W=(1/2)m(5²-3²)=(1/2)(1)(25-9)=8 J.

after.name: Question 14
after.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $1\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a resultant force. The particle's velocity is $(t+1)\,m/s,$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the work done by the force between the times $t=2\,s$ and $t=4\,s.$
after.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

The particle's velocity is given by $v(t)=t+1,$ where $t$ is time in seconds. So, the particle's initial velocity, at $t=2$, is

$$
{v}_{0}=v(2)=2+1=3\,m/s,
$$

and final velocity, at $t=4$, is

$$
{v}_{1}=v(4)=4+1=5\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =Δ\,\text{KE} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot (5)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot (3)^{2} \\  & =\frac{25}{2}-\frac{9}{2} \\  & =8\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

a

b
8J
c
16J
d
17J

EXPLANATION

The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

W=ΔKE

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

ΔKE=12mv12−12mv02

and m is the particle's mass, v0 is its initial velocity, and v1 is its final velocity.

The particle's velocity is given by v(t)=t+1, where t is time in seconds. So, the particle's initial velocity, at t=2, is v0=v(2)=2+1=3m/s, and final velocity, at t=4, is v1=v(4)=4+1=5m/s.

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

W=ΔKE=12⋅1⋅(5)2−12⋅1⋅(3)2=252−92=8J.

a
65J
b
51J
c
58J
d
46J
e
72J
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating acceleration gives v(t)=t²+1/t+C. Since v(1)=2, C=0, so v(2)=9/2 m/s. Work equals the kinetic energy change: W=(1/2)(8)((9/2)²-2²)=65 J.

after.name: Question 15
after.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $8\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a resultant force. The particle's acceleration is $(2t-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $t\ge 1$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=2\,m/s$ when $t=1\,s,$ calculate the work done by the force between the times $t=1\,s$ and $t=2\,s.$
after.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

The acceleration of the particle is given by $a(t)=2t-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},$ where $t$ is time in seconds.
We find the velocity $v(t)$ of the particle by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2t-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{2}+\frac{1}{t}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(1)=2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
2={1}^{2}+\frac{1}{1}+C\,⟹\,C=0.
$$

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)={t}^{2}+\frac{1}{t}.$
In particular, the particle's initial velocity, at $t=1,$ is

$$
{v}_{0}=v(1)=2\,m/s,
$$

and final velocity, at $t=2,$ is

$$
{v}_{1}=v(2)={2}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{9}{2}\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =Δ\,\text{KE} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 8\cdot {(\frac{9}{2})}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 8\cdot {2}^{2} \\  & =81-16 \\  & =65\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 15
?

A particle P of mass 8kg moves along the x-axis under the action of a resultant force. The particle's acceleration is (2t−1t2)m/s2, where t≥1 is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity v=2m/s when t=1s, calculate the work done by the force between the times t=1s and t=2s.

a
65J
b
51J
c
58J
d
46J
e
72J
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

W=ΔKE

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

ΔKE=12mv12−12mv02

and m is the particle's mass, v0 is its initial velocity, and v1 is its final velocity.

The acceleration of the particle is given by a(t)=2t−1t2, where t is time in seconds. We find the velocity v(t) of the particle by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫(2t−1t2)dt=t2+1t+C

To determine C, we use the fact that v(1)=2. Substituting this into the above gives

2=12+11+C⟹C=0.

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at time t is v(t)=t2+1t. In particular, the particle's initial velocity, at t=1, is v0=v(1)=2m/s, and final velocity, at t=2, is v1=v(2)=22+12=92m/s.

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

W=ΔKE=12⋅8⋅(92)2−12⋅8⋅22=81−16=65J.

content.knowledge_point: Applying the Work-Energy Principle To Find the Work Done by a Force
content.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $8\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a resultant force. The particle's acceleration is $(2t-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $t\ge 1$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=2\,m/s$ when $t=1\,s,$ calculate the work done by the force between the times $t=1\,s$ and $t=2\,s.$
content.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

The acceleration of the particle is given by $a(t)=2t-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},$ where $t$ is time in seconds.
We find the velocity $v(t)$ of the particle by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2t-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{2}+\frac{1}{t}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(1)=2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
2={1}^{2}+\frac{1}{1}+C\,⟹\,C=0.
$$

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)={t}^{2}+\frac{1}{t}.$
In particular, the particle's initial velocity, at $t=1,$ is

$$
{v}_{0}=v(1)=2\,m/s,
$$

and final velocity, at $t=2,$ is

$$
{v}_{1}=v(2)={2}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{9}{2}\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =Δ\,\text{KE} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 8\cdot {(\frac{9}{2})}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 8\cdot {2}^{2} \\  & =81-16 \\  & =65\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The work is W=∫₃⁵(x³-4) dx=[x⁴/4-4x]₃⁵=128 J. Using W=(1/2)m(10²-v₀²) gives 128=2(100-v₀²), so v₀²=36. The supplied positive initial velocity is 6 m/s.

after.name: Question 16
after.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $4\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of the force of magnitude $({x}^{3}-4)\,N$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, the particle was initially at $x=3$, and the particle has velocity $v=10\,m/s$ at $x=5,$ calculate the particle's initial velocity.
after.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=3$ to $x=5:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{3}^{5}({x}^{3}-4)\,\text{d}x \\  & =(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}-4x){|}_{3}^{5} \\  & =(\frac{625}{4}-20)-(\frac{81}{4}-12) \\  & =128\,J\end{aligned}
$$

The particle has velocity $v=10\,m/s$ at $x=5.$ So, we can find the velocity ${v}_{0}$ at $x=3$ using the work-energy principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =\frac{1}{2}{m}_{1}{v}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\ 128 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {10}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {v}_{0}^{2} \\ 128 & =200-2{v}_{0}^{2} \\ 2{v}_{0}^{2} & =72 \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =36 \\ {v}_{0} & =\pm 6.\end{aligned}
$$

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration. 

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at $x=3$ is $6\,m/s.$

after.html:
Question 16
?

A particle P of mass 4kg moves along the x-axis under the action of the force of magnitude (x3−4)N acting in the direction of increasing x. Given that x is measured in meters, the particle was initially at x=3, and the particle has velocity v=10m/s at x=5, calculate the particle's initial velocity.

a
6m/s
b
2m/s
c
7m/s
d
4m/s
e
8m/s
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

W=ΔKE

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

ΔKE=12mv12−12mv02

and m is the particle's mass, v0 is its initial velocity, and v1 is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from x=3 to x=5:

W=∫x1x2F(x)dx=∫35(x3−4)dx=(x44−4x)|35=(6254−20)−(814−12)=128J

The particle has velocity v=10m/s at x=5. So, we can find the velocity v0 at x=3 using the work-energy principle:

W=12m1v2−12mv02128=12⋅4⋅102−12⋅4⋅v02128=200−2v022v02=72v02=36v0=±6.

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration.

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at x=3 is 6m/s.

content.knowledge_point: Applying the Work-Energy Principle to Find a Particle's Velocity
content.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $4\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of the force of magnitude $({x}^{3}-4)\,N$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, the particle was initially at $x=3$, and the particle has velocity $v=10\,m/s$ at $x=5,$ calculate the particle's initial velocity.
content.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=3$ to $x=5:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{3}^{5}({x}^{3}-4)\,\text{d}x \\  & =(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}-4x){|}_{3}^{5} \\  & =(\frac{625}{4}-20)-(\frac{81}{4}-12) \\  & =128\,J\end{aligned}
$$

The particle has velocity $v=10\,m/s$ at $x=5.$ So, we can find the velocity ${v}_{0}$ at $x=3$ using the work-energy principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =\frac{1}{2}{m}_{1}{v}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\ 128 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {10}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {v}_{0}^{2} \\ 128 & =200-2{v}_{0}^{2} \\ 2{v}_{0}^{2} & =72 \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =36 \\ {v}_{0} & =\pm 6.\end{aligned}
$$

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration. 

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at $x=3$ is $6\,m/s.$

Question 17
?

A particle P of mass 1kg moves along the x-axis under the action of the force of magnitude (3x2+2)N acting in the direction of increasing x. Given that distances along the x-axis are measured in meters, the particle is initially at the origin, and the particle has velocity v=7m/s at x=2, find the particle's change in velocity in moving from x=0 to x=2.

a
3m/s
b
52m/s
c
4m/s
d
94m/s
e
2m/s
Submit

decision.explanation: The work is W=∫₀²(3x²+2) dx=[x³+2x]₀²=12 J. By the work-energy principle, 12=(1/2)(7²-v₀²), so v₀²=25 and v₀=5 m/s. The change in velocity is 7-5=2 m/s.

after.name: Question 17
after.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $1\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of the force of magnitude $(3{x}^{2}+2)\,N$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that distances along the $x$-axis are measured in meters, the particle is initially at the origin, and the particle has velocity $v=7\,m/s$ at $x=2,$ find the particle's change in velocity in moving from $x=0$ to $x=2.$
after.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=0$ to $x=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(3{x}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[{x}^{3}+2x]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =8+4-0 \\  & =12\,J\end{aligned}
$$

The particle has velocity $v=7\,m/s$ at $x=2.$ So, we can find the velocity ${v}_{0}$ at $x=0$ using the work-energy principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\ 12 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot {7}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot {v}_{0}^{2} \\ 12 & =\frac{49}{2}-\frac{1}{2}{v}_{0}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}{v}_{0}^{2} & =\frac{25}{2} \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =25 \\ {v}_{0} & =\pm 5.\end{aligned}
$$

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration. 

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at $x=0$ is $5\,m/s.$

Finally, the particle's change in velocity from $x=0$ to $x=2$ is

$$
{v}_{1}-{v}_{0}=7-5=2\,m/s.
$$

Question 17
?

A particle P of mass 1kg moves along the x-axis under the action of the force of magnitude (3x2+2)N acting in the direction of increasing x. Given that distances along the x-axis are measured in meters, the particle is initially at the origin, and the particle has velocity v=7m/s at x=2, find the particle's change in velocity in moving from x=0 to x=2.

a
3m/s
b
52m/s
c
4m/s
d
94m/s
e
2m/s
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

W=ΔKE

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

ΔKE=12mv12−12mv02

and m is the particle's mass, v0 is its initial velocity, and v1 is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from x=0 to x=2:

W=∫x1x2F(x)dx=∫02(3x2+2)dx=[x3+2x]02=8+4−0=12J

The particle has velocity v=7m/s at x=2. So, we can find the velocity v0 at x=0 using the work-energy principle:

W=12mv12−12mv0212=12⋅1⋅72−12⋅1⋅v0212=492−12v0212v02=252v02=25v0=±5.

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration.

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at x=0 is 5m/s.

Finally, the particle's change in velocity from x=0 to x=2 is v1−v0=7−5=2m/s.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms W=∫₀²(3x²+2) dx=12 J. Then 12=(7²-v₀²)/2 gives v₀=5 m/s, so the change in velocity is 7-5=2 m/s, option e.

content.knowledge_point: Applying the Work-Energy Principle to Find a Particle's Velocity
content.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $1\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of the force of magnitude $(3{x}^{2}+2)\,N$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that distances along the $x$-axis are measured in meters, the particle is initially at the origin, and the particle has velocity $v=7\,m/s$ at $x=2,$ find the particle's change in velocity in moving from $x=0$ to $x=2.$
content.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=0$ to $x=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(3{x}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[{x}^{3}+2x]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =8+4-0 \\  & =12\,J\end{aligned}
$$

The particle has velocity $v=7\,m/s$ at $x=2.$ So, we can find the velocity ${v}_{0}$ at $x=0$ using the work-energy principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\ 12 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot {7}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot {v}_{0}^{2} \\ 12 & =\frac{49}{2}-\frac{1}{2}{v}_{0}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}{v}_{0}^{2} & =\frac{25}{2} \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =25 \\ {v}_{0} & =\pm 5.\end{aligned}
$$

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration. 

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at $x=0$ is $5\,m/s.$

Finally, the particle's change in velocity from $x=0$ to $x=2$ is

$$
{v}_{1}-{v}_{0}=7-5=2\,m/s.
$$

Question 18

A particle P of mass 6kg moves along the x-axis under the action of a force of magnitude (8−x)N acting in the direction of increasing x. Given that x is measured in meters, and the particle has velocity v=6m/s at x=1, calculate the velocity of the particle at x=3.

a
210m/s
b
5m/s
c
25m/s
d
10m/s
e
22m/s
Submit

decision.explanation: The work is W=∫₁³(8-x) dx=[8x-x²/2]₁³=12 J. By the work-energy principle, 12=(1/2)(6)(v²-6²), giving v²=40. Since velocity remains positive, v=2√10 m/s.

after.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $6\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a force of magnitude $(8-x)\,N$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, and the particle has velocity $v=6\,m/s$ at $x=1,$ calculate the velocity of the particle at $x=3.$

$$

Question 18
?

A particle P of mass 6kg moves along the x-axis under the action of a force of magnitude (8−x)N acting in the direction of increasing x. Given that x is measured in meters, and the particle has velocity v=6m/s at x=1, calculate the velocity of the particle at x=3.

a
210m/s
b
5m/s
c
25m/s
d
10m/s
e
22m/s
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

W=ΔKE

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

ΔKE=12mv12−12mv02

and m is the particle's mass, v0 is its initial velocity, and v1 is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from x=1 to x=3:

W=∫x1x2F(x)dx=∫13(8−x)dx=[8x−x22]13=(24−92)−(8−12)=12J

The particle has velocity v=6m/s at x=1. So, we can find the velocity v1 at x=3 using the work-energy principle:

W=12mv12−12mv0212=12⋅6⋅v12−12⋅6⋅6212=3v12−1083v1=120v12=40v1=±40v1=±210.

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration.

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at x=3 is 210m/s.

content.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $6\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a force of magnitude $(8-x)\,N$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, and the particle has velocity $v=6\,m/s$ at $x=1,$ calculate the velocity of the particle at $x=3.$
content.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(8-x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[8x-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =(24-\frac{9}{2})-(8-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =12\,J\end{aligned}
$$

The particle has velocity $v=6\,m/s$ at $x=1.$ So, we can find the velocity ${v}_{1}$ at $x=3$ using the work-energy principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\ 12 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 6\cdot {v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 6\cdot {6}^{2} \\ 12 & =3{v}_{1}^{2}-108 \\ 3{v}_{1} & =120 \\ {v}_{1}^{2} & =40 \\ {v}_{1} & =\pm \sqrt{40} \\ {v}_{1} & =\pm 2\sqrt{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration. 

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at $x=3$ is $2\sqrt{10}\,m/s.$

Question 19

A particle P of mass 3kg moves along the x-axis under the action of the force of magnitude (2x2+x)N acting in the direction of increasing x. Given that x is measured in meters, the particle was initially at x=1, and the particle has velocity v=3m/s at x=4, calculate the particle's initial velocity.

a
15m/s
b
3m/s
c
35m/s
d
215m/s
e
33m/s
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

W=ΔKE

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

ΔKE=12mv12−12mv02

and m is the particle's mass, v0 is its initial velocity, and v1 is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from x=1 to x=4:

W=∫x1x2F(x)dx=∫14(2x2+x)dx=(x22−2x)|14=(8−12)−(12−2)=9J

The particle has velocity v=3m/s at x=4. So, we can find the velocity v0 at x=1 using the work-energy principle:

W=12m1v2−12mv029=12⋅3⋅32−12⋅3⋅v029=272−32v0232v02=92v02=3v0=±3.

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration.

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at x=1 is 3m/s.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms the work is 9 J. Thus 9=(3/2)(9-v₀²), giving v₀²=3 and the positive initial velocity √3 m/s, option b.

$$

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration. 

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at $x=1$ is $4\,m/s.$

A particle P of mass 7kg moves along the x-axis under the action of the force of magnitude (2x+3)N acting in the direction of increasing x. Given that x is measured in meters, the particle was initially at x=1, and the particle has velocity v=25m/s at x=3, calculate the particle's initial velocity.

a
7m/s
b
47m/s
c
8m/s
d
4m/s
e
6m/s
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

W=ΔKE

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

ΔKE=12mv12−12mv02

and m is the particle's mass, v0 is its initial velocity, and v1 is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from x=1 to x=3:

W=∫x1x2F(x)dx=∫13(2x+3)dx=(x2+3x)|13=(9+9)−(1+3)=14J

The particle has velocity v=25m/s at x=3. So, we can find the velocity v0 at x=1 using the work-energy principle:

W=12m1v2−12mv0214=12⋅7⋅(25)2−12⋅7⋅v0214=70−72v0272v02=56v02=16v0=±4.

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration.

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at x=1 is 4m/s.

content.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $7\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of the force of magnitude $(2x+3)\,N$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, the particle was initially at $x=1,$ and the particle has velocity $v=2\sqrt{5}\,m/s$ at $x=3,$ calculate the particle's initial velocity.
content.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(2x+3)\,\text{d}x \\  & =({x}^{2}+3x){|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =(9+9)-(1+3) \\  & =14\,J\end{aligned}
$$

The particle has velocity $v=2\sqrt{5}\,m/s$ at $x=3.$ So, we can find the velocity ${v}_{0}$ at $x=1$ using the work-energy principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =\frac{1}{2}{m}_{1}{v}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\ 14 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 7\cdot (2\sqrt{5})^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 7\cdot {v}_{0}^{2} \\ 14 & =70-\frac{7}{2}{v}_{0}^{2} \\ \frac{7}{2}{v}_{0}^{2} & =56 \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =16 \\ {v}_{0} & =\pm 4.\end{aligned}
$$

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration. 

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at $x=1$ is $4\,m/s.$
